selection.rule: Dependency-complete first 24 questions from the question-sheet selection order.

questions.question: What problem is being talked about at the start of this passage?
questions.answer: Being lazy or careless about worship, especially the required prayers.

questions.question: What does the passage say about the idea that all of a person’s time should go to worldly matters?
questions.answer: It says that idea is wrong because humans were not made only for this world.

questions.question: What do the examples about Saturn and the number of chickens in America teach?
questions.answer: They teach that people can waste precious time on useless facts while ignoring what matters most.

questions.question: What excuse is answered in the next part of the passage?
questions.answer: The excuse that necessary work and earning money leave no time for prayer.

questions.question: When should a person do the prayers according to this passage?
questions.answer: During times of rest, when the spirit can settle and the heart can breathe.

questions.question: What does the orchard represent in this part of the passage?
questions.answer: A person’s workplace and effort to make a living.

questions.question: How can a person change his own world?
questions.answer: By his heart, thinking, actions, and desires.

questions.question: What is the main message of this passage about worship and daily life?
questions.answer: A person should not let worldly busyness stop him from praying, because prayer brings great benefits in both worlds.

questions.question: What important question is asked to challenge those excuses?
questions.answer: Whether a person was created only for this world.

questions.question: In the worker example, what is being compared to the small wage loss?
questions.answer: The tiny worldly cost of taking time for prayer.

questions.question: Why are examples of faraway facts used?
questions.answer: To show how people waste time on matters that do not help their real purpose.

questions.question: How can prayer fit into a busy life according to the passage?
questions.answer: It can be done during breaks and moments of rest.

questions.question: What image is used for a person’s work life?
questions.answer: An orchard.

questions.question: What two broad kinds of livelihood are mentioned?
questions.answer: Worldly livelihood and the livelihood of the hereafter.

questions.question: What is the “true life” a person definitely has?
questions.answer: The present day.

questions.question: What should a regular person believe about his own prayer?
questions.answer: That it still carries real light and truth, even if it is not as strong as the prayer of great saints.

questions.question: Who is being addressed in this passage?
questions.answer: The soul that is too attached to worldly life.

questions.question: What basic life question does the passage raise?
questions.answer: Whether human beings were created only for worldly life.

questions.question: What does the sparrow example show about earning a living?
questions.answer: Even a tiny bird can manage its needs, so earning is not the whole purpose of being human.

questions.question: What does the passage say about many things people call “worldly occupations”?
questions.answer: Many are unimportant matters that people take on without real need.

questions.question: What can prayer make the world become?
questions.answer: A world full of light and meaning.

questions.question: What kind of soul is warned in this passage?
questions.answer: A soul that loves worldly life too much.

questions.question: Why is the example of the sparrow used?
questions.answer: It shows that even a small bird can manage worldly needs, so a human’s main job must be higher than just earning a living.

questions.question: What does the passage say about many activities people call important worldly work?
questions.answer: Many are actually small and unnecessary matters.
